Question Text: Three equal charges of +q are placed at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side 'a'. The magnitude of force on any one charge due to the other two is:
Concept / Formula: Use superposition: Find F from each of the two charges (both equal, angle 60° between them), then use vector addition. Since all charges equal and geometry symmetric: F_net = ?3·kq²/a².
Step-by-Step Solution:
Force from charge 2 on charge 1: F?? = kq²/a² (along one side)
Force from charge 3 on charge 1: F?? = kq²/a² (along other side)
Angle between F?? and F?? = 60°
F_net = ?(F??² + F??² + 2·F??·F??·cos60°)
= ?(1+1+1) · kq²/a² = ?3·kq²/a²
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: When three equal forces are at 120° to each other, they cancel to zero — that is a different configuration. Here forces are at 60° because the triangle is equilateral and both forces point AWAY from the central charge.

Question Text: Which of the following statements about electric field lines is INCORRECT?
Option A: They start from positive charges and end at negative charges
Option B: Two electric field lines can cross each other at a point of high field strength
Option C: The number of field lines per unit area indicates field strength
Option D: Field lines are always perpendicular to the surface of a conductor
Concept / Formula: Electric field lines NEVER intersect. If they did, at the intersection point the field would have two directions — which is physically impossible (field has unique direction at every point).
Step-by-Step Solution:
Check each statement:
A — Correct (positive ? negative)
B — INCORRECT. Lines never cross
C — Correct (density = field strength)
D — Correct (conductor surface is equipotential ? field perpendicular)
Answer: B
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: 'INCORRECT' questions require checking ALL options. Eliminate correct ones — the false statement is the answer. Field line crossing = two field directions at one point = impossible.

Concept / Formula: Gauss's Law: E inside a uniformly charged spherical shell = 0. All charge is on the surface; enclosed charge for any Gaussian surface inside = 0.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Q_enclosed = 0 (no charge inside the shell)
? = E·4?r² = Q_enclosed/?? = 0

Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Just OUTSIDE: E = ?/?? (or kQ/R²). Just INSIDE: E = 0. This is a classic trick — the word 'just inside' vs 'just outside' determines the answer.

Question Text: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the glass rod acquires a positive charge. This is because:
Option A: Protons are transferred from silk to glass
Option B: Electrons are transferred from glass to silk
Option C: Protons are transferred from glass to silk
Option D: Neutrons are transferred from glass to silk
Concept / Formula: Conservation of charge: Only electrons transfer in friction. Protons and neutrons are bound in the nucleus and cannot transfer. Object losing electrons ? positive charge.
Step-by-Step Solution:
Glass rod becomes positive ? it lost negative charge ? electrons left the glass.
Where did electrons go? To the silk.
Answer: Electrons transferred from glass to silk.
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Never say 'protons transfer' — protons are bound in the nucleus. In friction, always electrons move. The object that loses electrons becomes positive; the object that gains electrons becomes negative.

Question Text: Two identical conducting spheres carry charges of +6 ?C and ?2 ?C. They are brought into contact and then separated. The force between them at the original separation d is now:
Option A: Repulsive, equal to original attractive force
Option B: Attractive, half the original attractive force
Option C: Repulsive, one-third of the original attractive force
Option D: Repulsive, one-ninth of the original attractive force
Concept / Formula: When identical spheres touch: total charge redistributes equally. Q_total = +6 + (?2) = +4 ?C ? each gets +2 ?C. Calculate ratio of new force to original force.
Step-by-Step Solution:
Original: F? = k·6·2/d² = 12k/d² (attractive)
After contact: each = +2 ?C
New: F? = k·2·2/d² = 4k/d² (repulsive)
Ratio: F?/F? = 4/12 = 1/3
New force is 1/3 of original, and repulsive.
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: When two identical conductors touch: charges redistribute EQUALLY (not proportionally). Total charge = algebraic sum. Then split by 2. Sign of final charge determines attraction or repulsion.

Question Text: For an electric dipole of moment p, the ratio of electric field on the axial line to equatorial line at the same distance r (where r >> 2a) is:
Concept / Formula: E_axial = 2kp/r³ (along dipole axis). E_equatorial = kp/r³ (perpendicular to dipole). Ratio = 2:1.
Step-by-Step Solution:
E_axial = 2kp/r³
E_equatorial = kp/r³
Ratio E_axial:E_equatorial = 2kp/r³ : kp/r³ = 2:1
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: The axial field is TWICE the equatorial field at the same distance. Also: axial field is PARALLEL to dipole moment; equatorial field is ANTIPARALLEL to dipole moment.

Question Text: The electric potential at a point P, 20 cm from a charge of +4 ?C in vacuum is approximately:
Concept / Formula: V = kQ/r. Unlike field (vector), potential is scalar — just substitute and calculate.
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Potential is a SCALAR — no direction, no vector addition needed for multiple charges. Just add algebraically. Positive charge ? positive potential; negative charge ? negative potential.

Question Text: Which statement about equipotential surfaces is CORRECT?
Option A: Work done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface is maximum
Option B: Electric field can be parallel to an equipotential surface

Concept / Formula: Definition: Equipotential surface ? potential is same everywhere on it ? W = q·?V = q·0 = 0. Field is always perpendicular to equipotential surface, never parallel.
Step-by-Step Solution:
W = q(V_B ? V_A). On equipotential: V_A = V_B ? ?V = 0 ? W = 0.
Eliminate others:
A — Wrong: work is ZERO, not maximum
B — Wrong: field perpendicular, never parallel
C — Wrong: if they intersected, that point would have two potentials — impossible
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Equipotential surfaces never intersect (same reason as field lines). If they did, one point would have two different potential values — impossible. This is a direct parallel to field line logic.

Question Text: The force between two charges in vacuum is F. If the space between them is completely filled with a medium of dielectric constant K = 4, the force becomes:
Concept / Formula: F_medium = F_vacuum/K. Dielectric always REDUCES force between charges.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Dielectric reduces force by factor K. K is always ? 1 for any real material. K=1 for vacuum/air. Water has K?80 — charges attract 80x less in water than vacuum. This explains why ionic compounds dissolve in water.

Question Text: Two capacitors of 4 ?F and 6 ?F are connected in series across a 100 V supply. The voltage across the 4 ?F capacitor is:
Concept / Formula: In series: charge Q is same on both. V is shared inversely proportional to capacitance. Higher capacitance ? lower voltage.
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: In SERIES: Q is same, V divides INVERSELY to capacitance (opposite to resistors). In PARALLEL: V is same, Q divides proportionally to capacitance. Remember: capacitors are the OPPOSITE of resistors in series/parallel formulas.

Question Text: Which of the following is NOT a property of electric charge?
Concept / Formula: Three fundamental properties of charge: (1) Additive, (2) Quantised (Q=ne), (3) Conserved. Charge can be positive OR negative — there is no restriction.
Step-by-Step Solution:
Check each option:
A — Additive: TRUE (charges add algebraically)
B — Quantised: TRUE (Q = ne)
C — Always positive: FALSE (charges can be +ve or ?ve)
D — Conserved: TRUE (charge cannot be created or destroyed)
Answer: C
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: IMUCET frequently tests 'which is NOT correct' — read carefully. All three real properties (additive, quantised, conserved) are likely to appear together. The false option is usually about charge being only positive or only negative.

Question Text: A hollow metallic sphere is given a charge. Which statement is TRUE?
Option A: Charge distributes uniformly inside the sphere
Option B: Electric field inside the sphere is non-zero
Option C: All charge resides on the outer surface, field inside is zero
Concept / Formula: Key properties of conductors in electrostatics: (1) E=0 inside, (2) all charge on outer surface, (3) surface is equipotential, (4) potential inside = potential at surface (not zero).
Step-by-Step Solution:
A — False: charge is on the SURFACE, not inside
B — False: E = 0 inside a conductor
C — TRUE: all charge on outer surface, E=0 inside
D — False: potential inside = potential at surface (which is non-zero if charged)
Exam Tip / Common Mistake: Potential inside a charged hollow conductor = potential AT THE SURFACE (not zero). This is a very common wrong answer. E=0 inside ? V=0 inside. E = ?dV/dr = 0 means V is constant, not zero.
